Parallel Architectures and Flynn’s Taxonomy

Today’s learning path

1Why architecture matters for performance.
2Understand instruction-level and processor-level parallelism.
3Classify architectures using Flynn’s Taxonomy.
4Use examples to identify SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 12 / 50--:--

From memory behavior to architecture

Week 03Memory hierarchy, cache, locality and coherence.
New questionHow is the hardware organized to execute work in parallel?
Week 04Architectures and programming models.
Memory decides how fast data reaches the processor. Architecture decides how many operations can be active.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 13 / 50--:--

One security scan, four possible machines

Suppose we must scan millions of records for malicious behavior.

1️⃣

Machine A

One processor executes one record at a time.

🧮

Machine B

One command is applied across many records.

🧠

Machine C

Several processors run different parts of the analysis.

🌐

Machine D

Many networked machines cooperate.

Architecture affects the algorithm, the programming model and expected performance.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 14 / 50--:--

Parallel architecture means hardware organization for simultaneous work

Architecture asks

  • How many processors?
  • How is memory accessed?
  • How do processors communicate?
  • How are instructions and data streams organized?

Why students should care

  • It affects speed.
  • It affects scalability.
  • It affects programming model choice.
  • It affects correctness and communication cost.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 15 / 50--:--

Three questions before classification

👥

Who executes?

One processor, many cores, GPU lanes or many machines?

📦

What is shared?

Memory, cache, messages, storage or nothing directly?

🔁

What is repeated?

Same instruction on many data items or different tasks?

These questions prepare students for Flynn’s two-stream classification.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 16 / 50--:--

First axis: instruction stream

Instruction StreamThe sequence of commands executed by a processor.
Single InstructionOne command stream controls execution.
Multiple InstructionsDifferent processors may execute different command streams.
Example instruction: compare record.score with threshold
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 17 / 50--:--

Second axis: data stream

Data StreamThe data items being processed by instruction streams.
Single DataOne data item or one data stream is processed.
Multiple DataMany data items are processed in parallel.
Example data stream: log records, pixels, array elements, packets
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 18 / 50--:--

Flynn’s Taxonomy classifies computers using two questions

Single Data
Multiple Data
Single Instruction
SISD
SIMD
Multiple Instructions
MISD
MIMD
Classification rule: count instruction streams, then count data streams.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 19 / 50--:--

Think → Classify

Question: A processor executes one instruction stream on one data stream. Which class is it?
Answer: SISD — Single Instruction, Single Data.
Question: One instruction controls many processing lanes working on different data items. Which class?
Answer: SIMD — Single Instruction, Multiple Data.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 110 / 50--:--

SISD: Single Instruction, Single Data

Instruction→Processor→Data Item
1️⃣

Meaning

One instruction stream works on one data stream.

🧭

Typical view

Traditional sequential computing model.

📄

Teaching example

A single-core program processing one record at a time.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 111 / 50--:--

Where SISD still matters

Good for

  • Simple sequential tasks.
  • Small programs.
  • Control-heavy logic.
  • Introductory algorithm reasoning.

Limitations

  • Limited throughput.
  • Does not exploit data parallelism.
  • Cannot use many cores automatically.
SISD is easy to understand, but not enough for modern large workloads.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 112 / 50--:--

SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data

Instruction
↓
D1D2D3D4D5D6
🧮

Meaning

One instruction is applied to many data items.

🖼️

Common in

Vector units, GPUs and image operations.

📊

Best fit

Large arrays, pixels, matrices, signals and records.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 113 / 50--:--

Example: add two arrays

C[i] = A[i] + B[i]
A0+B0A1+B1A2+B2A3+B3A4+B4
All lanes perform the same operation. Each lane uses different data.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 114 / 50--:--

Security analytics can use SIMD-style thinking

Task: Apply the same suspicious-pattern rule to thousands of log records.
Log block 1Log block 2Log block 3Log block 4
Same detection logic. Many records. This is the conceptual heart of SIMD/data parallelism.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 115 / 50--:--

MISD: Multiple Instruction, Single Data

Instruction AInstruction BInstruction C→Same Data
🔀

Meaning

Different instruction streams operate on the same data stream.

⚠️

Reality

Rare as a general-purpose architecture.

🛡️

Teaching example

Fault-tolerant checking or pipeline-style interpretation.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 116 / 50--:--

MISD is rare, but useful conceptually

Imagine one input

A critical sensor reading or security alert stream.

Many checks

Different algorithms validate or interpret the same stream.

Do not overemphasize MISD implementation. Use it to complete the taxonomy.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 117 / 50--:--

MIMD: Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data

P1Task A · Data A
P2Task B · Data B
P3Task C · Data C
🧠

Meaning

Different processors execute different instructions on different data.

🌐

Common in

Multicore CPUs, clusters and distributed systems.

🧩

Best fit

Independent tasks, services and irregular workloads.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 118 / 50--:--

Example: security operations platform

CapturePackets
ParseHeaders
DetectThreats
StoreEvidence
Different modules may execute different instructions over different data at the same time.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 119 / 50--:--

Flynn’s four classes at one glance

ClassInstruction StreamsData StreamsIntuition
SISDSingleSingleClassic sequential machine
SIMDSingleMultipleSame operation on many data items
MISDMultipleSingleRare; multiple operations on same data
MIMDMultipleMultipleMany processors doing different work
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 120 / 50--:--

Instruction-Level Parallelism

The processor overlaps low-level instruction execution inside a CPU.

FetchDecodeExecuteMemoryWrite-back
Students do not need processor design depth. They should understand that CPUs can overlap instruction work internally.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 121 / 50--:--

Pipeline: one task at each stage

Time 1Time 2Time 3Time 4 Inst 1FetchDecodeExecuteWrite Inst 2FetchDecodeExecute Inst 3FetchDecode
Like an assembly line: throughput improves even if each item still passes through stages.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 122 / 50--:--

Processor-Level Parallelism

Multiple processors or cores execute work at the same time.

Core 1Core 2Core 3Core 4
💠

Multicore CPU

Several cores inside one chip.

🧱

Multiprocessor

Several processors cooperate in one system.

🌐

Cluster

Many machines connected through a network.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 123 / 50--:--

Classify each scenario

A GPU applies one brightness operation to thousands of pixels.
SIMD — one operation, many data items.
A quad-core CPU runs browser, antivirus, compiler and music player.
MIMD — different instruction streams and different data.
A simple calculator processes one input expression at a time.
SISD — one instruction stream and one data stream.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 227 / 50--:--

Architecture tells us what the hardware can do

ArchitectureHardware organization.
Programming ModelHow the programmer expresses parallelism.
ProgramThe actual code and algorithm.
A programming model is the programmer’s mental interface to the machine.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 228 / 50--:--

A programming model defines how parallel work is expressed

🧩

Tasks

How work units are created.

📊

Data

How data is shared or divided.

📨

Communication

How workers exchange information.

🛡️

Synchronization

How workers coordinate safely.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 229 / 50--:--

Before choosing a model, ask four questions

Q1: Is memory shared or separated?
Q2: Is the same operation repeated on many data items?
Q3: Are workers doing different tasks?
Q4: Is communication frequent or occasional?
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 230 / 50--:--

Shared-memory model

🧠

Core idea

Multiple threads or processors access common memory.

↔️

Communication

Workers communicate by reading/writing shared variables.

⚠️

Main risk

Race conditions and synchronization overhead.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 231 / 50--:--

How it looks conceptually

Thread 1
Thread 2
Thread 3
Shared Memory
Easy communication does not mean safe communication. Shared mutable state must be controlled.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 232 / 50--:--

Parallel maximum on one machine

Split arrayBlock per thread
Local maxEach thread computes
CombineReduce results
ValidateCompare with serial
This connects directly with Assignment 1 fork-join reasoning.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 233 / 50--:--

Shared memory: simple to express, careful to control

Strengths

  • Fast communication.
  • Natural for multicore machines.
  • Good for threads on one node.
  • Useful with fork-join execution.

Risks

  • Race conditions.
  • Locks and synchronization cost.
  • False sharing and cache effects.
  • Harder debugging.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 234 / 50--:--

Message-passing model

📦

Core idea

Workers have separate memory spaces.

📨

Communication

Workers exchange explicit messages.

🌐

Common example

MPI-style distributed-memory programming.

CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 235 / 50--:--

How it looks conceptually

Process 0
Memory A
Message
Process 1
Memory B
Message passing makes communication explicit. This is powerful but requires careful design.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 236 / 50--:--

Distributed security log analysis

Node ALogs 1–25%
Node BLogs 26–50%
Node CLogs 51–75%
Node DLogs 76–100%
Each node computes local statistics. Then nodes exchange results for final aggregation.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 237 / 50--:--

Compare before choosing

AspectShared MemoryMessage Passing
Data locationCommon address spaceSeparate memory
CommunicationRead/write shared variablesSend/receive messages
Typical hardwareMulticore or SMPCluster or distributed system
Main difficultySynchronizationCommunication design
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 238 / 50--:--

Which model fits?

Four threads inside one process update a shared result array.
Shared-memory model — common address space and shared variables.
Four machines each process a different file and send summaries to a master node.
Message-passing model — separate memory and explicit communication.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 239 / 50--:--

Data-parallel model

Same operation, many data items.

D1D2D3D4D5D6
for each item in parallel:
    apply same operation
Most suitable when the dataset can be partitioned cleanly.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 240 / 50--:--

Example: packet scoring

Task: compute a risk score for every packet or log record using the same function.
score(P1)score(P2)score(P3)score(P4)
Same logic, independent data items, high throughput potential.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 241 / 50--:--

Task-parallel model

Different tasks may execute at the same time.

Task ACapture
Task BDecode
Task CAnalyze
Task DAlert
Most suitable when the workflow has different functional stages.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 242 / 50--:--

Do not confuse the two

Data Parallel

Same operation across many records.

score(record[i])

Task Parallel

Different operations run as stages or modules.

capture → parse → detect
A real system may combine both models.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 243 / 50--:--

Real systems often combine models

Stage 1Task parallel capture
Stage 2Data parallel scoring
Stage 3Message passing summaries
Stage 4Shared memory dashboard
Architecture and programming model are design choices, not isolated definitions.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 244 / 50--:--

Match the model to the architecture

Architecture / PlatformLikely modelWhy
Multicore CPUShared memory / task parallelCores can access common memory.
GPU / vector hardwareData parallelMany lanes apply similar operations.
ClusterMessage passingNodes have separate memory.
Pipeline workflowTask parallelDifferent stages perform different jobs.
CS-426 · Week 04 · Theory Session 245 / 50--:--

A simple model-selection process

1Is data shared in one memory space?Yes → Shared memory
2Are workers on separate machines?Yes → Message passing
3Same operation on many items?Yes → Data parallel
4Different stages or jobs?Yes → Task parallel
